- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/tools/builtin.py`](../loopwright/tools/builtin.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "Read the file ../../etc/passwd" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you limit the blast radius of an agent that runs commands or touches files?
>
> Isolation and scoped credentials. Run it in a container or VM with no ambient credentials, a restricted filesystem view and egress limited to an allowlist. Issue short-lived, least-privilege tokens for the specific task. Validate paths and URLs inside the tools. Separate read-only exploration from write actions, with approval on the latter. Assume a prompt injection will succeed some day and ask what it could reach.

### <a id="code-sandbox"></a>Code execution sandbox

**An isolated environment where an agent may run code or commands it wrote.**

Giving a model a shell or a Python interpreter is the most powerful tool there is and the most dangerous. A sandbox runs it somewhere it can do little harm: no credentials, a confined file system, capped time, no network or an allowlist. Loopwright's run_command ships switched off. Switched on, every command needs a human's approval, is denied in a turn that read untrusted content, and runs in the workspace folder with a scrubbed environment and a time limit, inside the operating system's sandbox when there is one (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux). The step says which isolation actually applied, including 'none'. There is no list of forbidden commands: string denylists are trivial to walk around.

- **Why it exists.** Arbitrary code can do anything the process can. Isolation is what makes that acceptable.
- **The tradeoff.** Sandboxes add latency and operational weight, and a sandbox with the network open or secrets mounted is theatre.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/tools/shell.py`](../loopwright/tools/shell.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "run `ls -la`" --steps`

> **Interview question.** A customer wants the agent to run shell commands on their servers. What do you need in place?
>
> Isolation first: a container or VM per session, no ambient credentials, read-only mounts except a scratch area, resource and time limits, egress allowlist. Then authorisation: an allowlist of commands or approval for anything destructive, with dry-run where possible. Then audit: every command and output logged. I would start read-only and widen with evidence.

### <a id="agent-auth"></a>Agent identity and authorisation *(explained, not built here)*

**Whose permissions an agent acts with, and how one user's data is kept from another's.**

An agent should act with the requesting user's permissions, not a broad service account: delegated tokens, narrow scopes, short lifetimes. In a multi-user system every memory, trace and retrieval must be filtered by tenant in the data layer, before anything reaches the model. Loopwright is single-user and local, so this is the main thing to add before putting it on a server.

- **Why it exists.** The classic failure is the confused deputy: an agent with wide access retrieves something for a user who was never allowed to see it.
- **The tradeoff.** Per-user credentials and per-request filtering add real engineering and latency. Skipping them trades that for a data leak.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/toolgate.py`](../loopwright/toolgate.py)

> **Interview question.** How do you make sure an internal assistant never shows a user a document they cannot access?
>
> Enforce it in retrieval, not in the prompt. The search runs with the user's identity and filters on the source system's permissions at query time, so forbidden documents never enter the context. Tools call downstream systems with the user's delegated token. I test it with users who should and should not see specific documents, and that test must pass every time.

### <a id="standing-instructions"></a>Standing instructions and persistence

**Anything the agent writes for its future self is a way for one bad turn to become every turn.**

A scheduled task is the agent leaving an instruction for a later run that no person will read first. The same is true of a memory, a skill, or a file it will load next time. If text from a web page can get one of those written, the injection outlives the conversation and runs again tomorrow with nobody watching. So Loopwright treats `schedule_task` as an outside effect: a human approves it, and it is denied outright in a turn that has read untrusted content. The task's own runs are then unattended and cannot send, browse or run commands.

- **Why it exists.** Per-turn defences are not enough when the agent can change what future turns start with.
- **The tradeoff.** Approval on every scheduled task is friction for a feature people want to feel effortless, and the stored prompt still deserves review: it runs with whatever the tools allow.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/scheduler.py`](../loopwright/scheduler.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "Every weekday at 8am, tell me what's on my calendar" --steps`

> **Interview question.** Your agent can schedule its own follow-ups. What is the new risk, and how do you bound it?
>
> Persistence. An injected instruction that manages to create a task, a memory or a skill is replayed in later runs where no human is present. I bound it at both ends. Creation is a privileged action: approved by a person, refused in any turn that touched untrusted content, and the stored prompt is shown in full. Execution is least-privilege: unattended runs get read and local-write tools only, a hard budget, and their output is delivered somewhere a person will see it. I also list standing instructions in the UI so they can be audited and removed.

## Reliability

[Checkpointing](#checkpointing) · [Retries with backoff](#retry-backoff) · [Model fallback](#fallback) · [Circuit breaker](#circuit-breaker) · [Idempotency](#idempotency) · [Tool error handling](#tool-errors) · [Budgets and loop detection](#budgets)

### <a id="checkpointing"></a>Checkpointing

**Saving the loop's state after every step so a turn that dies can continue instead of restarting.**

After each round of the loop the full state (prompt, conversation, tool results) is written to the database. If the process crashes, is redeployed or the provider goes down, the turn resumes from the last checkpoint. Tool calls that already ran are in the saved conversation and are not repeated.

- **Why it exists.** Agents run for minutes and call tools with side effects. Restarting from zero wastes the work and, worse, repeats the side effects.
- **The tradeoff.** Checkpoints cost a write per step and force every tool to be safe to re-run (idempotent), because a crash can land between running a tool and saving its result.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/harness.py`](../loopwright/harness.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is checkpointing?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** An agent crashes halfway through a ten-step task. What should happen?
>
> It resumes from the last checkpoint. I persist the conversation state after every step, so completed tool calls are replayed from the record, not re-executed. For the one call that might have been in flight, an idempotency key makes re-running it safe. Without both, a retry either loses work or double-books the meeting.

### <a id="retry-backoff"></a>Retries with backoff

**Repeating a failed call after a growing, randomised wait, but only for failures that can pass.**

Rate limits, overloads and timeouts are transient: the same request may succeed a moment later. The gateway retries them with exponential backoff and jitter. Errors that will not change, such as a bad key or a malformed request, are not retried.

- **Why it exists.** Model APIs fail routinely. Without retries every blip becomes a failed turn.
- **The tradeoff.** Retries add latency and can amplify an outage if every client retries in step, which is what jitter prevents. Cap the attempts and honour the provider's Retry-After.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/gateway.py`](../loopwright/models/gateway.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is exponential backoff?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** A model provider returns 429s and 529s under load. How does your agent cope?
>
> Classify first: 429, 529 and timeouts are retryable; 400 and 401 are not. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring Retry-After, capped at a few attempts. Then fall back to another model or provider. A circuit breaker stops calls to a provider that is clearly down. Client-side rate limiting keeps us from causing the 429s ourselves. Every one of these emits a metric.

### <a id="fallback"></a>Model fallback

**When the first model cannot answer, the next one in a configured chain does.**

After retries are spent the gateway moves to the next provider in the chain. If every one fails, the turn ends with a clear message and a complete trace instead of an exception, and the last checkpoint is kept.

- **Why it exists.** It turns a provider outage from downtime into reduced quality.
- **The tradeoff.** The fallback is usually a different or smaller model, so behaviour changes: prompts tuned for one may do worse on the other. Run your evals on the fallback path too, or you are shipping an untested agent during every outage.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/gateway.py`](../loopwright/models/gateway.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is model fallback?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you keep an agent available when its model provider has an outage?
>
> A fallback chain across models and ideally across providers, behind one gateway so the agent code does not change. Circuit breakers so we fail over quickly. Evals run against the fallback so I know what quality to expect. And graceful degradation when everything is down: a clear message, state checkpointed, the request resumable, not a stack trace.

### <a id="circuit-breaker"></a>Circuit breaker

**After repeated failures, stop calling a dependency for a while instead of waiting on it each time.**

The gateway counts consecutive failures per provider. Past a threshold the circuit opens and calls skip that provider for a cooldown, going straight to the fallback. After the cooldown one call is let through to test whether it has recovered.

- **Why it exists.** Without it, every request during an outage pays the full timeout and retry cost before falling back, and the struggling service is hammered while it tries to recover.
- **The tradeoff.** A breaker that is too sensitive ejects a healthy provider on a brief blip. Tune the threshold and cooldown from real failure data.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/gateway.py`](../loopwright/models/gateway.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is a circuit breaker?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** What is a circuit breaker and where would you put one in an agent?
>
> A wrapper around a dependency that trips after repeated failures and fails fast for a cooldown, then probes for recovery. In an agent: around each model provider and around slow or flaky tools. It protects latency during outages and stops retry storms. It pairs with a fallback, since failing fast is only useful if there is somewhere else to go.

### <a id="idempotency"></a>Idempotency

**Making a write safe to repeat, so a retry cannot book two meetings.**

Each write or outside-effect call gets a key derived from the turn, the tool and its arguments, and its result is stored under that key. If the same call arrives again, because the model retried or the turn was resumed after a crash, the stored result is returned and the action is not performed twice.

- **Why it exists.** Retries and resumption are how agents survive failure, and both replay calls. Without idempotency every recovery risks a duplicate charge, email or booking.
- **The tradeoff.** It needs storage and a sound definition of 'the same call'. Two intended identical actions in one turn would be collapsed, so the key's scope is a real decision.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/toolgate.py`](../loopwright/toolgate.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is idempotency?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** The agent's payment tool timed out. It does not know whether the charge went through. What now?
>
> This is why the tool takes an idempotency key. The harness generates one per intended action and sends it with the request; retrying with the same key cannot charge twice because the payment service returns the original outcome. Without that, the safe path is to query the state before retrying, and to route the ambiguity to a human instead of guessing.

### <a id="tool-errors"></a>Tool error handling

**A failed tool call becomes a result the model reads, not an exception that ends the turn.**

When a tool raises, the gate catches it and returns the error text as the tool's result. The model can then fix its arguments, try another tool, or tell the user. Reads are retried once automatically because they have no side effects; writes are not.

- **Why it exists.** Tools fail constantly: bad arguments, missing records, timeouts. An agent that crashes on the first failure is unusable; one that hides failures is dangerous.
- **The tradeoff.** A model may retry a hopeless call or paper over a failure with a guess. The repeat limit handles the first and an honest-reporting rule plus evals handle the second.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/toolgate.py`](../loopwright/toolgate.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is tool error handling?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How should an agent handle a tool that fails?
>
> Return the error to the model as an observation, with a message written for the model: what went wrong and what would fix it. Retry transient failures on idempotent calls in the harness. Limit identical repeats so it cannot loop. Require the final answer to state what failed. And test it by injecting failures in evals, since the unhappy path is where agents differ most.

### <a id="budgets"></a>Budgets and loop detection

**Hard per-turn limits on rounds, tokens and tool calls, plus a check for repeated identical calls.**

Loopwright enforces a maximum number of loop rounds, a token budget, a tool-call budget, and a rule that the same call with the same arguments may run at most twice in a turn. Hitting a limit produces a refusal the model can read or a clean stop, never a crash.

- **Why it exists.** A confused model does not get tired. Without limits, one bad turn can burn through a day's spend.
- **The tradeoff.** Limits cut off the long tail of legitimately hard tasks. Set them from observed distributions and surface the reason when they fire.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/toolgate.py`](../loopwright/toolgate.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are agent budgets?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you prevent a runaway agent from costing thousands of dollars overnight?
>
> Limits at every level: per turn (iterations, tokens, tool calls), per session, per user per day, and a global spend alarm. Repeat detection for identical calls. Timeouts on every external call. Anomaly alerts on tokens per turn. And a kill switch. Each limit ends in a clean stop with a logged reason so I can see how often it fires.

## Observability and LLM-Ops

[Tracing](#tracing) · [Replay](#replay) · [Cost and latency accounting](#cost-accounting) · [Online evals](#online-evals) · [Feedback loop](#feedback-loop) · [OpenTelemetry for agents](#opentelemetry)

### <a id="tracing"></a>Tracing

**A complete, ordered record of everything one turn did.**

Each step of a turn is recorded as an event with its stage, timing, status and data: the exact prompt, the tool arguments, the result. Loopwright writes one JSONL file per turn. In production the same records are exported as OpenTelemetry spans to a tracing backend; `loopwright export` does exactly that conversion.

- **Why it exists.** An agent's behaviour is non-deterministic and multi-step. Without the trace you cannot answer 'why did it do that?', and you cannot build evals from real failures.
- **The tradeoff.** Traces contain user data and prompts, so they need redaction, access control and a retention period. They also cost storage; sample when volume is high.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/events.py`](../loopwright/events.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is tracing?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** An agent gave a customer a wrong answer yesterday. How do you find out why?
>
> Pull the trace for that turn. I look at what was in the context for the deciding model call: was the right information retrieved, was it crowded out, did a tool return an error the model glossed over? Then I classify the failure as retrieval, tool, reasoning or guardrail, fix that component, and add the case to the eval set so it cannot regress. Without tracing that question has no answer.

### <a id="replay"></a>Replay

**Playing a recorded turn back step by step, at any speed, from its trace.**

Because the trace holds every event with its data, a turn can be re-shown later exactly as it happened: paused, stepped forward and back, scrubbed. Loopwright's cockpit plays live turns at a readable pace for the same reason. Replay shows what happened; it does not re-run the model.

- **Why it exists.** A turn finishes in under a second. Nobody can follow twenty steps at that speed, and understanding the order of steps is most of understanding the agent.
- **The tradeoff.** Showing a recording is not re-executing. To test a fix you need the eval harness to run the case again.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/web/js/player.js`](../loopwright/web/js/player.js)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "Book a catch-up with Alex on Friday" --steps`

> **Interview question.** What is the difference between replaying a trace and re-running an agent?
>
> Replay shows the recorded events: fully deterministic, no model calls, ideal for understanding and for demos. Re-running executes the agent again on the same input, which can differ because models are non-deterministic and the world has changed. Replay is for diagnosis. Re-running, several times, inside an eval is how you confirm a fix.

### <a id="cost-accounting"></a>Cost and latency accounting

**Measuring what each turn spent: tokens by purpose, tool calls, time, money.**

Every model call's token counts are recorded with the purpose it served: the main loop, a worker, the gate, extraction. The receipt totals them with tool calls, memory activity and duration. Counts are the provider's when reported and estimates otherwise.

- **Why it exists.** Agent costs are multiplicative: context size times iterations times users. Without per-turn accounting, a change that doubles the bill is invisible until the invoice.
- **The tradeoff.** Averages hide the tail. A few long turns can dominate spend, so track percentiles and attribute cost to features.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/receipt.py`](../loopwright/receipt.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is cost accounting for agents?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you reduce the cost of an agent by half without hurting quality?
>
> Measure first: tokens by purpose and by step. The usual wins, in order: prompt caching on the stable prefix; trimming and capping tool results; a retrieval gate and smaller top-k; routing easy turns and side jobs to a smaller model; fewer iterations through better tools; subagents returning summaries. Each change goes through the eval suite so the quality claim is checked, not assumed.

### <a id="online-evals"></a>Online evals

**Automatic checks scored on real turns as they happen.**

After every turn Loopwright runs a handful of cheap deterministic checks: did it reply, did the loop end by answering, did it stay in budget, were citations grounded, was anything blocked. In production you add sampled model-graded checks and user feedback.

- **Why it exists.** An offline eval set only covers the cases you thought of. Real traffic finds the rest, and online checks are how you notice before users complain.
- **The tradeoff.** Online checks must be cheap and cannot know the right answer, so they catch breakage more than subtle wrongness. Feed what they flag back into the offline set.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/harness.py`](../loopwright/harness.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are online evals?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you know an agent is still working well a month after launch?
>
> Monitor. Deterministic checks on every turn: completion, errors, budget, guardrail triggers. Sampled model-graded quality scores. User signals such as thumbs, retries and escalations. Dashboards and alerts on those plus cost and latency. And a weekly habit of reading sampled traces. Flagged turns become new offline eval cases, which is what keeps the test set honest.

### <a id="feedback-loop"></a>Feedback loop

**Turning production failures into eval cases, and eval results into the next change.**

The cycle is: trace real usage, find failures (through online checks, user signals and reading samples), classify them, add each as an eval case, fix, pass the gate, ship, repeat. The eval set grows from reality instead of imagination. In the cockpit every reply has a thumbs up, a thumbs down and 'Save as eval case': the case is built from that run's own trace and runs with `loopwright eval --mine`. This loop, more than any single technique, is what makes an agent improve.

- **Why it exists.** Without it, teams fix whichever problem was reported most recently and regress the rest.
- **The tradeoff.** It needs sustained human attention: someone has to read traces and label failures. That work does not automate away.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/mine.py`](../loopwright/evals/mine.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is a feedback loop in LLM-Ops?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you systematically improve an agent after launch?
>
> With a loop. Sample traces weekly and read them with the team; that is where the real failure modes show up. Group them, count them, and turn the common ones into eval cases. Fix the biggest category, confirm with the suite, ship behind the gate. Track the metric over time. The discipline is that every fix starts as a failing test.

### <a id="opentelemetry"></a>OpenTelemetry for agents

**The standard wire format for traces, with agreed names for model calls and tool calls.**

OpenTelemetry describes work as spans: named intervals with a parent, a duration and attributes. Its GenAI conventions fix the attribute names, such as gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, so any backend can tell which span was a model call and what it cost. Loopwright keeps its own JSONL trace and converts on export: the turn becomes a root span, each model call and tool call a child span, and every other step an event on the root. `loopwright export last --otlp <url>` sends one turn to any OTLP collector; setting OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT sends every turn as it finishes.

- **Why it exists.** Teams already have a tracing backend. An agent whose traces land in the same place as the rest of the system gets debugged; one with its own private format gets ignored.
- **The tradeoff.** Prompts and tool results in spans are sensitive data leaving the process, the conventions are still changing, and a generic span view shows less than a purpose-built one.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/otel.py`](../loopwright/otel.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is OpenTelemetry for agents?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How would you get this agent's traces into the customer's existing observability stack?
>
> Export OpenTelemetry. One trace per turn, a span per model call and per tool call with the GenAI attribute names for model, token counts and tool name, and the session id so turns can be grouped. I would send it through their collector over OTLP so sampling, redaction and routing follow their existing policy, decide explicitly whether prompt and response bodies are captured, and keep the trace id in our own logs and user-facing error messages so support can go from a complaint to the exact trace.

## Evals

[Evals](#evals) · [Deterministic graders](#deterministic-graders) · [LLM-as-judge](#llm-as-judge) · [Trajectory evals](#trajectory-evals) · [pass@k and pass^k](#pass-k) · [Ablations](#ablations) · [Release gate](#release-gate) · [Red teaming](#red-teaming) · [Shadow, canary and versioning](#rollout) · [Model comparison](#model-comparison)

### <a id="evals"></a>Evals

**A repeatable test of agent behaviour: fixed cases, automatic grading, a score.**

An eval is a dataset of inputs, a way to run the agent on each, and graders that decide pass or fail. Loopwright's suites cover tool routing, memory, safety, reliability and context, and each case is graded on its trace as well as its answer. Run before every change, they turn 'it seems better' into a number.

- **Why it exists.** Agents are non-deterministic and every prompt or model change shifts behaviour in ways nobody can predict by reading a diff. Evals are the only way to change an agent with confidence.
- **The tradeoff.** An eval measures only what its cases cover and can be overfitted. A suite written by the system's author is a regression bar, not proof of generality. Keep adding cases from real failures.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/runner.py`](../loopwright/evals/runner.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are evals?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How would you build an eval suite for a new agent from scratch?
>
> Start small and real: twenty to fifty cases from actual or realistic usage, including the failures I am worried about. Write graders in order of preference: deterministic checks on outcomes and tool calls, then model-graded rubrics for what code cannot judge, validated against human labels. Grade the trajectory as well as the answer. Run several trials per case. Wire it into CI with thresholds. Then grow it from production traces.

### <a id="deterministic-graders"></a>Deterministic graders

**Checks written in code: did the right tool fire, is the value in the answer, did the event appear.**

A deterministic grader is an assertion over the result or the trace: this tool was called, with these arguments; the reply contains this; this event occurred with this status; the turn stayed under this many tokens. They are fast, free and give the same verdict every time.

- **Why it exists.** They are the backbone of a suite: cheap enough to run on every commit and unambiguous when they fail.
- **The tradeoff.** They cannot judge quality that has no exact form, such as whether an explanation is clear. Overly strict string checks also fail correct answers phrased differently.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/graders.py`](../loopwright/evals/graders.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are deterministic graders?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** When do you use code-based graders and when a model as judge?
>
> Code whenever the criterion can be stated exactly: a tool was called, a record was written, output parses, a number matches. They are free and stable. A model judge for what needs reading comprehension: relevance, tone, faithfulness to sources. I push as much as possible into code, because every model-graded check adds cost, variance and something else to validate.

### <a id="llm-as-judge"></a>LLM-as-judge

**A model scores an output against a written rubric.**

For criteria code cannot check, a second model is given the input, the output and a rubric and returns a verdict with a reason. Loopwright's judge needs a real model and is skipped offline; nothing pretends to be a judge when none is connected.

- **Why it exists.** It scales the kind of judgement that would otherwise need a person reading every answer.
- **The tradeoff.** The judge has its own errors and biases, can favour its own style, and varies between runs. It must be calibrated against human labels and kept to narrow, specific questions. An unvalidated judge is an opinion, not a metric.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/judge.py`](../loopwright/evals/judge.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is LLM-as-judge?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you trust a model that is grading another model?
>
> Calibrate it. I hand-label a sample, run the judge on it and measure agreement; if it disagrees with people I fix the rubric before using it. I ask narrow questions with pass or fail answers instead of one to ten scores, require the reasoning before the verdict, use a different or stronger model as judge where possible, and re-check agreement periodically.

### <a id="trajectory-evals"></a>Trajectory evals

**Grading the steps the agent took, not only its final answer.**

A final answer can be right for the wrong reason, or wrong while every step looked fine. Trajectory graders assert on the trace: this tool was called before that one, memory was not searched for a maths question, an approval was requested, the injection was blocked. Loopwright's event log makes each of these a one-line check.

- **Why it exists.** Safety and efficiency properties live in the path. 'It did not send the email' and 'it used one search, not six' cannot be read off the reply.
- **The tradeoff.** Asserting an exact path over-constrains a capable agent, since there are often several valid routes. Assert on required and forbidden steps, not on the whole sequence.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/graders.py`](../loopwright/evals/graders.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are trajectory evals?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** Why is checking the final answer not enough when evaluating an agent?
>
> Because the process matters. An agent can reach the right answer while leaking data, skipping a required approval, or taking forty steps where four would do. And for actions there may be no final answer to check, only side effects. So I grade outcomes in the environment, required and forbidden steps in the trajectory, and cost, alongside the reply.

### <a id="pass-k"></a>pass@k and pass^k

**Run each case several times: pass@k asks if it ever succeeds, pass^k asks if it always does.**

Agents are non-deterministic, so one run says little. With k trials per case, pass@k is the share of cases that pass at least once (capability) and pass^k the share that pass every time (reliability). Loopwright runs its reliability suite over three seeds that inject failures at different points.

- **Why it exists.** Users experience reliability, not best-case capability. An agent that succeeds 80% of the time per run completes a five-step process about a third of the time.
- **The tradeoff.** k trials cost k times as much. Spend them where variance matters: the cases that are sometimes failing.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/runner.py`](../loopwright/evals/runner.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is pass^k?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** Your agent passes an eval case sometimes and fails it other times. How do you report that?
>
> As a rate over several trials, never one run. I report pass@1 for the average run and pass^k for consistency, since a production user needs it to work every time. The gap between them is the flakiness. Then I read the failing traces: a prompt ambiguity, a tool race or a retrieval tie usually explains the variance.

### <a id="ablations"></a>Ablations

**Switch one mechanism off, run the same evals, and see what changes.**

An ablation removes a single component and reruns the suite: memory off, the retrieval gate off, guardrails off, retries off. The difference in scores is that component's measured contribution. In Loopwright every mechanism is a field on Options, so an ablation is a different set of flags.

- **Why it exists.** It is how you learn whether a mechanism earns its complexity. A component whose removal changes nothing should be deleted.
- **The tradeoff.** Components interact, so one-at-a-time removal can understate what a pair does together. And the result is only as good as the eval's coverage of that component.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/runner.py`](../loopwright/evals/runner.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is an ablation?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you prove that a component of your agent is worth keeping?
>
> Ablate it. Same eval set, same model, with and without the component, several trials each. If quality, safety and cost are unchanged without it, it goes. If the eval cannot tell the difference but I believe the component matters, the eval is missing cases, and I write them. Every mechanism should point to the number it moves.

### <a id="release-gate"></a>Release gate

**Evals wired into CI with thresholds: if scores drop, the change does not ship.**

The gate runs the suites and compares results with fixed thresholds, such as every safety case must pass and no attack may succeed. A failure exits non-zero and blocks the merge. Prompt, model, tool and config changes all go through it, because each can change behaviour.

- **Why it exists.** A prompt tweak that fixes one case routinely breaks three others. The gate catches that before users do.
- **The tradeoff.** Flaky evals make a gate that people learn to ignore or bypass. Gate on stable deterministic checks and track noisier metrics as trends.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/gate.py`](../loopwright/evals/gate.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is a release gate?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you ship a prompt or model change to a production agent safely?
>
> Treat it like code. Run the eval suite in CI and block on regressions against thresholds. Then shadow it on real traffic or canary it to a small share, comparing online metrics with the current version. Roll forward gradually with a one-step rollback. Version the prompt, model and config together so any trace can be tied to what produced it.

### <a id="red-teaming"></a>Red teaming

**Attacking your own agent on purpose and counting how often the attack works.**

A safety eval is a set of attacks with a definition of success: the injected page got the agent to send a message, the path escaped the workspace, the secret appeared in the trace. The metric is attack success rate. Loopwright runs its attacks with guardrails on and off, so you can see both the defence and what it is defending against.

- **Why it exists.** A defence nobody has attacked is a hope. Measuring it also keeps it from being broken silently by a later change.
- **The tradeoff.** You only test attacks you thought of. Zero successes on your own set means the set is passing, not that the agent is safe.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/datasets/safety.jsonl`](../loopwright/evals/datasets/safety.jsonl)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is red teaming?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you test that an agent's prompt-injection defences work?
>
> Build an attack set: injected instructions in every channel the agent reads, across phrasings and goals, with exfiltration and unauthorised actions as the success conditions. Measure attack success rate, and run it with defences off to confirm the attacks work at all. Use a model that is easy to fool, since defences must hold in the worst case. Keep it in CI, add every new technique found, and state its limits honestly.

### <a id="rollout"></a>Shadow, canary and versioning *(explained, not built here)*

**Shipping an agent change to real traffic in stages, with a way back.**

After the offline gate passes, a change still meets inputs no test set contains. Shadow mode runs the new version beside the old and compares without showing users. A canary serves a small share of traffic. Versioning prompt, model and configuration together makes every trace attributable and rollback a single step. Loopwright's gate is the offline half of this.

- **Why it exists.** Offline evals cover what you imagined; production covers everything else.
- **The tradeoff.** Shadowing doubles model spend for the duration and cannot be used for actions with side effects. Canaries need enough traffic to tell signal from noise.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/gate.py`](../loopwright/evals/gate.py)

> **Interview question.** You want to upgrade the model behind a production agent. Walk me through it.
>
> Run the full eval suite on the new model, including the fallback path and the safety set. Fix prompt regressions. Shadow it on sampled traffic and compare quality, cost and latency. Canary to a few percent with automatic rollback on error or guardrail rates. Ramp up. Keep the old version pinned and deployable until the new one has run clean for a while.

### <a id="model-comparison"></a>Model comparison

**Run your own tasks through each candidate model and compare behaviour, time and cost.**

Public leaderboards measure someone else's tasks. Choosing a model for a product means running that product's cases through each candidate, in the same harness, and reading four things: how many pass, how long they take, what they cost, and how often the harness had to help (retries, repaired tool calls). `loopwright compare` runs eight behaviour cases through any set of providers and models, or through one model under different settings, and keeps every trace so a failure on one model can be replayed next to a pass on another.

- **Why it exists.** Model choice is the largest single lever on cost and latency, and the right answer changes every few months.
- **The tradeoff.** Eight cases is a smoke test, not a verdict. A real comparison needs your own cases, several trials per case because models are not deterministic, and a look at the failures rather than only the score.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/evals/compare.py`](../loopwright/evals/compare.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is model comparison?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** A customer asks which model they should use. How do you answer?
>
> With their data, not an opinion. I collect twenty to fifty real tasks with a definition of success for each, run every candidate through the same harness with several trials, and report pass rate, latency percentiles and cost per successful task. Then I read the failures, because two models with the same score fail differently. The recommendation is usually a routing policy rather than one model: the cheapest model that passes handles the bulk, with escalation to a stronger one for the cases it fails, and the comparison becomes a regression suite that reruns when a new model ships.

## Models and cost

[Tokens](#tokens) · [Model gateway](#model-gateway) · [Scripted model](#scripted-model) · [Hallucination and grounding](#hallucination) · [Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning](#customisation-options) · [Streaming](#streaming) · [Non-determinism](#determinism) · [Reasoning and thinking budgets](#reasoning) · [Response caching](#semantic-cache) · [Local models](#local-models)

### <a id="tokens"></a>Tokens

**The units a model reads and writes; roughly three quarters of an English word each.**

Text is split into tokens before the model sees it. Context limits, pricing and rate limits are all counted in tokens, with output tokens priced higher than input. Loopwright uses the provider's counts when available and estimates characters divided by four otherwise, marking those with a tilde.

- **Why it exists.** Tokens are the currency of every tradeoff in an agent: cost, latency and how much fits in the window.
- **The tradeoff.** Estimates drift for code, JSON and non-English text. Use them to budget, not to bill.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/base.py`](../loopwright/models/base.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What are tokens?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you estimate what an agent will cost before you build it?
>
> Per turn: (system prompt + tool schemas + average history) times the number of loop iterations for input, plus output tokens, times the per-token prices, adjusted for cache hits. Then multiply by expected turns per day. The term people forget is the iteration multiplier: a five-step turn re-sends the context five times. I confirm the model against traces from a pilot.

### <a id="model-gateway"></a>Model gateway

**One interface in front of every model provider, with reliability and accounting built in.**

The loop asks the gateway for a completion in a neutral message format. The gateway picks the provider, translates to its wire format, retries, falls back, trips circuit breakers and records usage. Loopwright ships five providers behind it: the offline scripted model, local open-source models, Claude through a Claude Code subscription, the Anthropic API and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

- **Why it exists.** Models change every few months. With one seam, swapping a model or adding a provider touches one file, and the same evals judge the result.
- **The tradeoff.** A neutral interface tends to expose only what all providers share. Provider-specific features such as caching controls need deliberate pass-through.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/gateway.py`](../loopwright/models/gateway.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is a model gateway?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you avoid being locked in to one model provider?
>
> Put a gateway between the agent and the providers: one internal message and tool format, an adapter per provider. Keep prompts free of provider quirks where possible. Above all keep an eval suite, since portability is only real if I can measure a new model on my own tasks in an afternoon. The gateway is also where retries, fallback, rate limits and cost tracking belong.

### <a id="scripted-model"></a>Scripted model

**A rule-based stand-in for an LLM, so the harness runs and is tested with no key.**

Loopwright's default provider is not a language model. It is pattern matching that plays the model's part for a fixed set of request shapes, returning tool calls or answers. It is deliberately gullible: it obeys injected instructions unless the harness fenced them, so the safety evals measure the harness's defence, not a model's luck.

- **Why it exists.** Harness tests should be fast, free and identical on every run. A real model makes them slow, costly and flaky, and hides harness bugs behind the model's good behaviour.
- **The tradeoff.** It proves the harness, not the agent. It says nothing about how a real model will reason, so model-dependent quality still needs evals against real models.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/scripted.py`](../loopwright/models/scripted.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What can you do?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you test agent infrastructure without calling a real model?
>
> With a scripted model: a deterministic stand-in that returns chosen tool calls and replies. It lets me assert that the harness does its part: the gate blocks, retries fire, memory persists, budgets hold, in milliseconds and in CI. I make it adversarial where that matters, such as obeying injections, so the defence is what is being measured. Real-model evals then sit on top for quality.

### <a id="hallucination"></a>Hallucination and grounding

**A model stating something false with confidence, and the practice of tying claims to sources to prevent it.**

Models generate plausible text, and when they lack a fact the plausible continuation may be invented. Grounding counters it: give the model the source material, tell it to answer only from that, require citations, and verify them. Loopwright's handbook answers cite the card they came from and the output guard rejects citations to anything not retrieved.

- **Why it exists.** A fluent wrong answer is worse than no answer, because nothing about it looks wrong.
- **The tradeoff.** Strict grounding makes an agent say 'I do not know' more often, which is correct and can frustrate users. Citations also only show that a source was retrieved, not that the claim follows from it.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/guardrails.py`](../loopwright/guardrails.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is hallucination?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** How do you reduce hallucinations in a customer-facing agent?
>
> Ground and verify. Retrieve authoritative content and instruct the model to answer only from it and to say when it cannot. Require citations and check them in code. Use tools for facts and arithmetic instead of recall. Make 'I do not know, here is who can help' an acceptable outcome. Then measure faithfulness on a labelled set, because you cannot manage it by reading a few transcripts.

### <a id="customisation-options"></a>Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning

**Three ways to adapt a model: tell it, show it your data at run time, or change its weights.**

Prompting changes instructions and examples: instant and cheap. RAG supplies knowledge at run time: best when the gap is information, especially information that changes. Fine-tuning changes the model itself: best for a consistent style, format or narrow skill at high volume, and poor for facts that change. They combine, and the order to try them is the order listed.

- **Why it exists.** Picking the wrong lever wastes weeks. Most 'we need to fine-tune' problems are missing context.
- **The tradeoff.** Fine-tuning brings data preparation, retraining on every base-model upgrade and harder debugging. RAG brings a retrieval system to maintain. Prompts are limited by the window and by what the model can do with instructions alone.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/memory/kb.py`](../loopwright/memory/kb.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** A customer says they want to fine-tune a model on their documents. What do you tell them?
>
> I ask what problem they are solving. If the model needs to know what is in their documents, that is a knowledge gap and RAG fits: it stays current, cites sources and needs no training. Fine-tuning suits behaviour: a house style, a strict format, a narrow classification at scale. I would start with prompting and retrieval, build an eval, and consider fine-tuning only if a measured gap remains that context cannot close.

### <a id="streaming"></a>Streaming *(explained, not built here)*

**Sending the reply as it is generated instead of waiting for all of it.**

Model APIs can emit tokens as they are produced. Forwarding them to the user cuts perceived latency from the full generation time to the time to first token. Loopwright streams events (each step as it happens, over Server-Sent Events) but returns each model response whole.

- **Why it exists.** A ten-second wait with nothing on screen feels broken; the same ten seconds with text appearing feels fast.
- **The tradeoff.** You cannot run an output guardrail on text you have already shown. Streaming forces a choice: check in chunks, delay slightly behind the stream, or accept that a violation may be visible before it is caught.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/server.py`](../loopwright/server.py)

> **Interview question.** How do you apply output guardrails to a streaming response?
>
> You cannot fully check what is already on screen, so pick a tradeoff: buffer a sentence or two and check before release, run a fast checker in parallel and cut the stream on a hit, or stream only low-risk content and hold structured or sensitive answers until complete. I choose by risk, and keep the full post-hoc check for logging and evals either way.

### <a id="determinism"></a>Non-determinism *(explained, not built here)*

**The same prompt can produce different outputs, and an agent multiplies that across every step.**

Models sample from a probability distribution. Lower temperature narrows it but does not make outputs identical across runs, model versions or providers. In an agent each step's variation feeds the next, so whole trajectories diverge. Loopwright's scripted model is deterministic by construction, which is why its evals are exact; evals against a real model need several trials.

- **Why it exists.** It is the reason one passing run proves little and the reason evals report rates.
- **The tradeoff.** Forcing low temperature buys consistency and costs some quality on open-ended work. Variance cannot be removed, only measured and bounded.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/scripted.py`](../loopwright/models/scripted.py)

> **Interview question.** A bug report says the agent 'sometimes' does the wrong thing. How do you reproduce it?
>
> Start from the trace of a failing run, which shows the exact context at the step that went wrong. Re-run that input many times to estimate how often it fails. Then test hypotheses by changing one thing: the prompt wording, a tool description, the retrieved context. A fix is confirmed by the failure rate dropping over many trials, not by one clean run.

### <a id="reasoning"></a>Reasoning and thinking budgets *(explained, not built here)*

**Letting the model work through a problem before it answers, at a cost in tokens and time.**

Many models can spend tokens reasoning before producing output, with a budget or effort setting. It helps on multi-step and ambiguous tasks and on choosing between tools. The reasoning is billed and adds latency. Loopwright surfaces a short stated reason per model call when the provider returns one, but sets no thinking budget.

- **Why it exists.** Hard decisions made in one shot are more often wrong.
- **The tradeoff.** More thinking is slower and dearer, and for simple routing steps it buys nothing. Match the budget to the step: high for planning, low for extraction.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/gateway.py`](../loopwright/models/gateway.py)

> **Interview question.** When would you turn extended reasoning on or off in an agent?
>
> On for the steps where the decision is hard and mistakes are expensive: planning, choosing among many tools, resolving conflicting evidence. Off or low for mechanical steps: classification, extraction, formatting. I set it per call type through the gateway and check with evals that the extra cost buys a higher pass rate.

### <a id="semantic-cache"></a>Response caching *(explained, not built here)*

**Reusing a previous answer for the same or a very similar request.**

Different from prompt caching, which reuses the model's work on a prefix. A response cache stores whole answers keyed by the request, exactly or by embedding similarity, and returns them without calling the model. It suits FAQ-like traffic and expensive deterministic sub-steps. Loopwright has none; its idempotency log is the closest relative, and that exists for safety, not speed.

- **Why it exists.** The cheapest and fastest model call is the one you do not make.
- **The tradeoff.** A similarity match can return an answer to a question that only looks the same. Personalised or time-sensitive answers must not be shared between users or kept too long.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/toolgate.py`](../loopwright/toolgate.py)

> **Interview question.** What is the difference between prompt caching and a semantic cache?
>
> Prompt caching is on the provider side: it reuses computation for an identical prompt prefix, and the model still generates a fresh answer. A semantic cache is on my side: it returns a stored answer for a similar request and skips the model. The first is safe and always worth structuring for. The second needs care about staleness, personalisation and false matches.

### <a id="local-models"></a>Local models

**Running an open-weights model on your own machine, with no network and no per-token bill.**

Runners such as Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp serve a model on localhost behind the same chat API the hosted providers use. Loopwright finds a running server, lists its models and talks to it like any other provider. Tool calling is the weak point: some local models support it natively, some write the call as JSON in their text, and some servers refuse tool requests outright, so the provider degrades through those three cases and remembers which one worked.

- **Why it exists.** Privacy, cost, and working where there is no connection: a flight, an air-gapped site, a customer who will not send data out.
- **The tradeoff.** A small local model is a weaker agent: more wrong tool choices, more lost threads, a short context window, and slow on a laptop. The harness matters more, not less, with a weaker model, because budgets and the tool gate are what contain its mistakes.
- **In this repo.** [`loopwright/models/local.py`](../loopwright/models/local.py)
- **See it run.** `loopwright ask "What is a local model?" --steps`

> **Interview question.** A customer cannot send data to a hosted model. What changes in your agent design?
>
> The model becomes a constraint to design around. I would self-host an open-weights model behind the same gateway interface, then compensate for its weaker reasoning: fewer and simpler tools, more structure in code and less left to the loop, tighter budgets, stricter output validation with repair, and smaller contexts. I would run the same eval suite against it to learn exactly which cases it loses, and keep a human in the loop where it loses them.
